Issued at 342 AM CDT Fri Sep 11 2026

     TODAY THROUGH SUNDAY...

Early this morning, upper air analysis shows a weak shortwave trough 
over the Ozarks, and the region's next system over the PNW. At 
the surface, a weak surface ridge is stretched out across 
eastern Kansas. Light winds, clear skies, and a very moist 
boundary layer from yesterday's rainfall are contributing to 
patchy fog across eastern Kansas and western Missouri. With 
diurnal heating after sunrise, much of this fog should mix out 
by mid-morning, and mostly clear skies will dominate the region 
this afternoon and evening with afternoon highs returning into 
the 90s.

Scattered thunderstorms are expected across the Dakotas and Nebraska 
this evening into tonight ahead of the next deep layer trough 
traversing eastward over the Rockies. A cluster of showers and 
storms is likely to be over southern Nebraska late tonight, and
this the point where uncertainty in the forecast remains quite 
high. Over the past 2-3 days, mid-range global models were on 
board with this cluster of storms diving southward and feeding 
off of a stout nocturnal LLJ along with ample elevated 
instability across Kansas. However, the latest CAMs are 
significantly more bearish; showing a decaying cluster of 
showers barely making it into portions of central Kansas
by Saturday morning. This is likely due to the short-range 
models having a better handle on the strength and positioning of
the nocturnal LLJ late tonight into Saturday morning, generally
keeping it much weaker and further west across the High Plains.
Because of this trend, POPs have been lowered significantly for
overnight tonight into Saturday morning.

Meanwhile, a surface frontal boundary will sag into northern/central 
Kansas by Saturday afternoon with ample instability along and 
south of the front (over 2000 J/kg of SBCAPE). Convergence along
the front, along with a very subtle shortwave trough 
approaching the region, will support development of widely 
scattered showers and storms across the northern half of Kansas 
Saturday afternoon and evening. Effective shear will be in the 
neighborhood of 35-40 knots supporting the potential for 
organized convection. In addition, model soundings show an 
inverted-v profile across much of the forecast area Saturday 
afternoon and early evening. Given these conditions, any storm 
that develops could be strong to marginally severe with large 
hail and damaging wind gusts possible. There is an outside 
chance of a tornado given low-level shear along the frontal 
boundary, but LCLs will be comically high (some model soundings 
show potential cloud bases near 3km), so chances of a tornado or
two remain very low.

Lastly, another round of isolated to scattered storms are possible 
Saturday night into Sunday morning along the mid-level baroclinic 
zone. At the moment, the mid-level baroclinic zone (and accompanying 
WAA) is forecast to be across central Kansas. Any storms that 
develop are likely to be elevated. Environmental shear and 
instability support the potential for organized convection capable 
of large hail and maybe some localized damaging wind gusts. 
Generally speaking, storm chances will come to an end Sunday morning 
as mid-level WAA wanes across the forecast area. The aforementioned 
frontal boundary is expected to wash out by Sunday, and hot weather 
is forecast to briefly make a return Sunday afternoon with highs in 
the mid 90s to potentially low 100s.

     MONDAY THROUGH THURSDAY...

The forecast for next week generally remains on track as of now. Mid-
range guidance continues to show a more robust trough digging into 
the Rockies and Great Plains by the beginning of the work week next 
week which could potentially lead to another period of active 
weather. It's a bit too early to get into the finer details at time; 
however, it appears increasingly probable that a cold front will 
stall out across Kansas Monday night after another potentially
hot day on Monday. This could lead to potentially several 
rounds of showers and storms through much of next week. Heavy 
amounts of rainfall don't appear to be on the table at this 
time. That being said, meaningful rainfall across drought 
stricken areas remains possible. In addition to the potential 
for rainfall, cooler temperatures are still forecast, though 
temperatures have trended slightly warmer than in previous 
forecasts. Still, a prolonged stretch of highs in the 80s will 
provide a much needed break from the heat.
